claims.text: The nanoparticles are AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The initial nanoparticles are smaller than 5 nm and have an FCC crystal structure.
Thermal instability in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles is driven by surface-energy gradients and differential vapor pressures rather than sluggish diffusion.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than Co, Ni, and Pt.
Au and Cu have higher vapor pressures than Co, Ni, and Pt under the relevant heating conditions.
The surface-energy and vapor-pressure differences cause Au and Cu to segregate to nanoparticle surfaces at elevated temperature.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-5 nm particles kinetically favors surface segregation.
In sub-5 nm particles, surface-energy minimization dominates configurational-entropy stabilization.
The mechanism becomes dominant at approximately 600 K.
Above approximately 600 K, the surface-diffusion activation barrier is overcome and rapid elemental migration to the surface occurs.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu subsequently evaporate.
Au and Cu evaporation causes particle-size reduction and reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries.
Heating produces progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles and widening of the particle-size distribution.
Icosahedral particles have higher surface energy than truncated-octahedral particles.
Icosahedral particles segregate and reshape more rapidly than truncated-octahedral particles.
The proposed mechanism is dominant in sub-10 nm nanoparticles because surface-energy terms are critical at that scale.
The proposed mechanism is less relevant in larger nanoparticles, where bulk properties dominate.
The prevailing explanation is that high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize the FCC structure against coalescence and segregation.

contradictions.description: The proposed test is described as determining whether surface-energy gradients alone explain phase separation, but the specified simulations include both surface-energy gradients and differential vapor pressures. A successful simulation would therefore test the combined mechanism, not surface-energy gradients alone.
